headline: Kids Build Robots to Save Native American Languages
meta_description: Danielle Boyer created SkoBots—small robots shaped like woodland creatures—to help Native American children learn languages nearly lost to boarding school assi…
summary_short: A 25-year-old entrepreneur created SkoBots—shoulder-sized robots decorated in Native American florals—to help children learn endangered languages through programming.
body:
Danielle Boyer, a member of the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, watched her grandmother become one of the last fluent speakers of their dialect of Anishinaabemowin as generations of Native children lost their languages to the U.S. Indian boarding school system. Determined to reverse this loss, Boyer created SkoBots at age 18—small robots shaped like woodland creatures, decorated with Native American florals, small enough to sit on a shoulder. Children program these robots to answer questions in their own languages. Ask a SkoBot what bear is, and it responds in Anishinaabemowin: "makwa." Now 25, Boyer has mentored hundreds of Native American children across the country in building and programming their own SkoBots.

One of them is 12-year-old Holden Hoy, an Ojibwe student at JKL Bahweting Anishinaabe School in Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, who named his robot Sabe—the word for Bigfoot in Anishinaabemowin, representing honesty in Ojibwe culture. Boyer deliberately rejected generative AI for the SkoBots, after watching ChatGPT invent fake words in Anishinaabemowin. Instead, the robots run on pre-recorded audio triggered by keywords—no synthetic speech, no artificial invention. "If we're not learning our language correctly, we shouldn't learn it at all," Boyer said.

The real impact extends beyond the robots themselves. Holden's mother, Jocelyn, had once rejected her Native American identity but now eagerly learns alongside her son. As Holden put it simply: "The language is the culture."
quick_facts: Danielle Boyer created SkoBots at age 18, now mentors hundreds nationally
Fewer than 10,000 people in the U.S. speak Anishinaabemowin
12-year-old Holden Hoy programmed his robot Sabe at Michigan school
SkoBots use pre-recorded audio, not AI, to preserve accurate language
